ML based method · Digital twin: five years, 579 wells, Bengaluru-calibrated

Five years of history for every well, on a Bengaluru-calibrated twin, and a ML forecaster that reads each well's own physics.

The company's real records cover two weeks. Forecasting from one day to twelve weeks ahead needs years: several monsoons, several dry seasons, and the slow decline in between. So we built a physics twin of the fleet, five years long — six kinds of well, paved city wards, real Bengaluru rain, and recharge checked against published Bengaluru observations — and tested the forecaster on it blind.

What we have, what we built, what we test

Vendor export

A 14.5-day export

579 wells, 15–29 July 2026, in the vendor's file format. Its level values are demonstration data: it gives us the format and each well's operating pattern, not a real level history.

Digital twin

A five-year twin of the fleet

579 simulated wells, hour by hour, August 2021 to July 2026, driven by real IMD rainfall for Bengaluru: six kinds of well, 198 paved wards, 739 links between neighbours, sensor noise and faults. It writes files in the exact vendor format.

Known answer

The pipeline, run blind

The forecaster sees only the files and public rainfall. Its forecasts are scored against the twin's hidden truth — true levels, traits, links and recharge — which only the scorer reads.

The data: a Bengaluru twin of the fleet

A simulator, not a dataset. Each well is a two-store reservoir: a fast store that the pump draws down and that recovers when it stops, and a slow store, the resting level of the surrounding rock. Its hidden traits are drawn once — resting level, refill time τ, drawdown per cubic metre a, pump rate and efficiency, intake depth, and a fracture zone below which drawdown steepens — and the water level is then integrated hour by hour under rain, pumping, neighbours and a sensor model.

1 · Six kinds of well

Each well is first given a hidden kind, chosen for Bengaluru's two-layer hard-rock setting (a weathered top layer over fractured basement) and for valley versus ridge position; its traits are then drawn from that kind's ranges. No model sees the kind.

SW-R shallow weathered, ridge5850 m7 h0.35 m8–15 d0.6
DF-V deep fractured, valley14570 m14 h0.45 m10–20 d1.3
DF-R deep fractured, ridge173120 m25 h0.55 m15–25 d1.3
LY low-yield deep58150 m35 h0.90 m20–30 d1.3

Kind medians; each well's values are lognormal around them. Fracture-zone and intake depths, soil-bucket capacity (100–200 mm) and recharge delay come from the kind's ranges. The neighbour graph has a fleet mean of 2.5 links per well; the link factor scales a kind's chance of a link.

2 · Rain: Bengaluru's own

IMD 0.25° gridded daily rainfall for Bengaluru, June 2021 to July 2026, so every monsoon and every dry spell in the twin happened. The four full years average 1,199 mm (1,946 mm in 2022, 893 mm in 2023), against a CGWB normal of 831 mm.

3 · Terrain: paved wards

The city is divided into 198 wards. Each ward's sealed share is drawn between 60 % and 95 % (mean 82 %; an IISc study puts Bengaluru at 78 % paved in 2017), and each well sits in a ward.

4 · How rain reaches the aquifer

Rain on a ward's open ground enters a soil bucket (100–200 mm, losing 2.25–3.75 mm a day to evapotranspiration), and 30 % of the bucket's overflow reaches the aquifer. Rooftop rainwater harvesting sends 0–20 % of each well's rain (drawn per well); leaking mains and sewers add 0.05 mm a day; lakes add 0.5 mm a day at 10 % of wells. Every route passes through the well's own recharge delay.

5 · Pumping and dry runs

Each well pumps on its own pattern from the export: sessions per day, start hours, durations, scaled by season and cut on supply-outage days. When the level reaches the intake the pump runs dry and the controller locks it out. Five years produced 147,155 dry-run events in 336 wells.

6 · Wells that affect each other

A hidden graph of 739 links joins neighbours. Water flows along each link in proportion to the difference in the two wells' drawdowns, so a pumping well drags its neighbours down and an idle one lets them recover. The model never knows who is connected to whom.

7 · What the sensors see

The true level is never written to the observed files. The forecaster gets what the vendor's sensors would record: a level at the start and stop of each session with ±0.2 m noise, 0.5 % outlier readings, 3 % missing well-days, telemetry every five minutes, and faults on 10 % of wells.

Output: 1,174,683 sessions and 32.8 million telemetry rows over five years, in the vendor's exact file format; true levels, traits, links and recharge kept as hidden truth.

Recharge checked against published Bengaluru observations

The leakage and harvesting settings were set against published Bengaluru observations, with pass bands fixed before anything was measured, and chosen from 36 combinations by a fixed rule. No forecast score entered the choice.

CheckPublishedPass bandTwin
Rain-driven recharge, share of annual rain13.5 % rainfall recharge factor, 2016 (Sekhar et al., Sustainability 2018)9–18 %10.0 %
Total recharge, share of annual rain—≤ 25 %13.0 % (156 mm a year)
Recharge in the wettest two months67 mm, August–September 2017 (Sekhar et al.)33–135 mm82 mm (Aug–Sep 2022)
Shallow wells, May to November level rise0.18–5.89 m rise in shallow wells (CGWB, Bangalore Urban)0.2–6.0 m, majority rising1.69 m, 73 % rising
Deep wells, May to November level rise—reported0.85 m

Of the 156 mm of recharge a year, 120 mm is driven by rain and 36 mm is constant. In a city 82 % sealed, infiltration through open soil barely registers — raising it from 30 % to 90 % changed rain-driven recharge by 0.001 % of rain — so rain reaches the aquifer mainly through harvesting.

Two stress tests: non-linear well loss and neighbour interference

Two further twins test the forecaster where the world departs from its physics. Each is built from the same reference twin — the typed, paved twin before the recharge calibration — with exactly one change, so any difference in the results has one cause.

Quadratic well loss

Real borewells lose extra head at the well face that grows with the square of the discharge (Jacob's s = BQ + CQ²). The forecaster's physics core has only the linear term. In the test twin every well gets a C·Q² loss, with C drawn per well so that the loss at rated discharge is 20–50 % of the well's linear drawdown: a median 11.1 m at rated discharge, and 68 % of the drawdown seen in a stop reading. The loss enters what the sensors and the pump see — stop readings, telemetry, pump head — and nothing else, so the aquifer, the sessions, the dry runs and the true resting levels are identical to the reference twin, verified file by file.

Neighbour interference: the counterfactual

The reference twin's 739 links are switched off (conductance zero, graph and random draws kept, verified by a control rebuild that reproduces the reference byte for byte), the feature table is rebuilt on the new observations, and the existing models are applied unchanged.

The forecaster in four steps

A physics core makes the first guess; a learning layer corrects it; calibration makes the range honest.

  1. Read each well's physics from its own records. From the files alone, the feature build derives 225 columns per well-day (924,015 well-days), with each well's τ, a and resting level fitted from its own sessions over a rolling 60 days.
  2. Two equations give the first guess.
    hrest = hs + (hstop − hs) · e−rest/τ
    Recovery, pump off: the gap to the resting level closes at the well's own pace τ.
    deepest = hrest + a · Q · τ · (1 − e−t/τ)
    Drawdown, pump on: a session of length t at rate Q deepens the level toward a limit set by a, Q and τ.
  3. A learning layer predicts the core's residual. LightGBM models: 21 daily models (days 1–7 × quantiles 0.1, 0.5, 0.9) that use the operator's pumping plan for the coming week, and 24 weekly models (weeks 1, 4, 8 and 12 × the same quantiles, with and without per-well memory) that use each well's last 28 days of pumping and the season's typical rain. The weekly forecast is of the well's average resting level over the target week.
  4. Calibrate the range. Conformal calibration sets the 80 % and 90 % bands per horizon and season on the calibration year; the offsets are then applied unchanged to the test year.

The known-answer test

Because the twin's traits are hidden, we can ask whether the features recover them from the sensor files alone: the same step the pipeline will perform on real wells.

How it was tested

SplitWalk-forward only: train August 2021 – July 2024; calibrate on August 2024 – July 2025; test once on August 2025 – July 2026, with a forecast every Monday. Unseen wells116 wells held out of training entirely and scored separately. BaselineDoing nothing: the level stays where it was last seen. Truth firewallNothing in the feature or model code reads the hidden truth; only the scorer does.
Where every number comes from

Every figure on these pages is on the twin, with ±0.2 m level noise. No real level measurement was used.

See the results →

Borewell Forecast is a proof of concept for forecasting groundwater levels in Bengaluru borewells. Results are labelled by where the data came from: vendor export (15 days, July 2026, in the vendor's real format but with demonstration water-level values), synthetic test system (450 simulated wells with a known answer) or digital twin (physics-based simulations of the 579 wells: one year in iteration 1, five years in later iterations and in Stage 2). No real water-level measurement has been used yet, and nothing here is yet a validated field forecast. Built by the FARII consortium.
